newsitem.title: USA: Virtual pet craze spawns ad, licensing schemes.
newsitem.headline: Virtual pet craze spawns ad, licensing schemes.

text.p: With virtual pets hatching this spring faster than parents can say "Tamagotchi," makers of the keychain toys are scrambling to assemble advertising and line up licensing partners.
Tokyo-based Bandai Co. Ltd., maker of the Tamagotchi, the original virtual pet, has shipped 10 million units globally since last November, when it began selling the microchip "pets."

In the United States Bandai has shipped 3.5 million of the toys since their May launch, said Gene Morra, vice president of marketing for Bandai America Inc., based in Cerritos, Calif. "Worldwide, we've already shipped more than Beanie Babies and Tickle Me Elmo combined," Morra said.

Bandai, which also marketed the Mighty Morphin Power Rangers action figures, is putting its licensing machine into motion, with nearly two dozen licensing deals already inked, including a deal with a top-tier, fast-food chain, Morra said. He declined to disclose the name of the fast food marketing partner.

Though word of mouth has been the most effective means of moving his product -- in Japan, where the craze originated, the company has done no advertising -- Morra says Bandai is readying a national TV campaign to break Sept. 1 targeting family prime time TV.

The back-to-school ads, from Bandai ad agency J. Walter Thompson USA, Chicago, a unit of WPP Group, will tout upcoming product enhancements, including changes in the programming, game play and graphics. "We have an obligation to keep this fresh, interesting and collectible," he said of the changes.
The toy is a hand-held, keychain-size electronic game that mimics the life, and death, of a pet. By pressing buttons, the owner can feed it, play with it, clean up after it and put it to bed.

Initially, Bandai had expected the toys, which retail for around $15, to appeal mainly to young teenage girls in the United States. "The basic play pattern we're gratifying here is nurture," Morra said.
However, early sales trends already reveal a much wider appeal for the toy, with the primary user having an average age of 19, with equal interest from both sexes.

As a result, Bandai has shifted its TV media targets from programming geared to young teens, such as that on Nickelodeon, to MTV and prime time network TV. "When you have something that acts like a real pet, you're going to touch the inner child in everybody," Morra explained.

With its appeal to the difficult-to-reach older teen market, virtual pets will attract a wide range of toymakers, said Frank Reysen, editor of Playthings magazine. "Virtually everybody in the industry will get into it. It's going to be a growing and highly competitive market," he said.

Tiger Electronics, based in Vernon Hills, Ill., is pursuing that market aggressively with its Giga Pet, which will be in full national distribution by the end of the first week in June, said Lana Simon, a spokeswoman for Tiger. Sold in six varieties, Giga Pets retail for $9.99.
Sales of its product have been brisk. At an opening May 29 at FAO Schwarz in Chicago, Tiger sold about 1,500 Giga Pets within two hours of the store's opening.

Tiger has no immediate plans to launch an ad campaign, said Marc Rosenberg, vice president of marketing. Instead, he said, Tiger is capitalising on its existing movie licensing agreements, producing a Baby T-Rex pet from this summer's "Jurassic Park" sequel, "The Lost World," and an upcoming pet tied to Walt Disney's "101 Dalmatians."

In addition, Tiger has lined up a fourth-quarter promotional deal with PepsiCo's KFC Corp. that features a special edition Giga Pet available with purchase. Tiger also will take advantage of its strategic alliance with Nabisco Foods, planning a holiday-themed joint promotion featuring 13 of Nabisco's cookie brands. TV advertising will support both of those promotions, Rosenberg said.
Posnick & Kolker, New York, handles advertising for Tiger.

Playmates Toys, maker of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, plans to set its Nano Pal pets apart by narrowing its target to girls aged 9 to 13, said Gina Beebe, vice president of marketing for girls toys for the Costa Mesa, Calif.-based company. In addition to its puppy and kitty pets, Playmates also sells a human baby version of the toy. "That's something that the competition does not have," Beebe said.

Playmates, which uses a fashion-oriented positioning intended to appeal to its teen-girl target, began shipping its Nano Pals nationally last week. The pets are encased in the latest trendy colours: chartreuse, orange, purple and a pearlized clear. They sell for $14.99 to $19.99.

TV ads from Sachs Group, Los Angeles, break June 16 in Cincinnati, Columbus and Indianapolis. National TV will begin June 30. Like Bandai and Tiger, Playmates also is considering a number of licensing opportunities, Beebe said.

For retailers, at least, it seems the more virtual pets, the merrier. At Pittsfield, Mass.-based retailer Kay-Bee Toy Stores, which sells all three of the virtual pets, the three brands so far are selling equally well, said spokeswoman Raili Filion. "The preference is for Tamagotchi, but if the other pet is there, it will sell just as quickly," Filion said.
